Elijah-Craig-Barrel-Proof-s-First-Batch-:
The year’s first batch of Elijah Craig Barrel Proof has hit the shelves. This one is aged for 10 years and 9 months before being bottled at cask strength,  which in this case was 59.5% ABV. Batch A124 is the first of three to come this year, with the remaining releases B and C slated for May and September.

While owner Heaven Hill’s distillers aim for flavor consistency with the Elijah Craig batches, no two expressions will be identical—a fact of life for any batch series. But that’s a good thing, as fans like to explore the nuances of each. Certainly you can count on big bourbon flavors—vanilla, toasted oak, butterscotch, caramel, baking spice, and a hint of fruitiness by way of apple and orange.

Each Elijah Craig Barrel Proof batch is distinguished by a letter and three numbers. The letter, which will be either an A, B, or C, refers to the first, second, or third release of the year, while the first number refers to the month, and the latter two to the year. 

The whiskey has developed a cult following, and for good reason—most of the batches we’ve scored have consistently earned scores of 93 or higher. Batch B517 represented a high point, becoming our Whisky of the Year in 2017. When it won that award, the price was just $60 a 750 ml. Six years later, even amid a dizzying upward spiral in whisky prices, Heaven Hill has pretty much held the line, at least in comparison to many other players. With its $75 price tag, the new Elijah Craig Barrel Proof is once again very likely to over-deliver on value.
whisky-lovers-travel-guide-to-british-co:
From a distance, Victoria, BC has all the hallmarks of a sleepy government town, from its quaint, cozy bistros and boutiques to its easily strollable downtown and the eye-catching turquoise domes of the 19th-century Parliament buildings. But up close, this scenic provincial capital offers more for lovers of quality beers and spirits than meets the eye.

A visit to Victoria should begin at the city’s original brewpub, Spinnakers, perched spectacularly above Lime Bay and only a short drive or 25-minute waterside walk from downtown’s Harbour Airport. Known locally as “Spins,” Spinnakers was born as a British-style pub and brewery, but since its founding in 1984 it has expanded to include a restaurant, guest suites, a bottle shop, and most recently, a distillery.

Although many of Spinnakers’ spirits are produced from 100% malted barley, just like its Mitchell’s Extra Special Bitter and Nut Brown ales, you won’t find any single malt whisky in its cellar. Instead, there is the bright and pleasantly phenolic Knot single malt spirit, aged 18 months in the brewery’s charred stout casks, hence not old enough to be called whisky, as well as Chocoholic crème de cacao, a complex, not-too-sweet chocolate liqueur made from the same malt spirit that’s been macerated with spent cacao husks from a local chocolatier before being sweetened and proofed to 25% ABV.

A short walk from Spinnakers is Driftwood Brewery and Distillery, home to the unapologetically old school Fat Tug IPA. Fat Tug is ubiquitous in Victoria—and throughout southern British Columbia, for that matter— so it’s best to focus on the brewery’s ever-evolving slate of seasonal and limited releases, as well as the distillery’s pair of gins and unique Oyster Spirit, a creamy, briny clear liquor infused with whole oysters.

Crossing the harbor on the Johnson Street Bridge, you come to the city’s finest beer bar, the comfortably rustic Drake Eatery, where spirits take a back seat to 29 rotating taps of British Columbia beer, and the menu is so local that it lists the names of many of the ingredient growers and suppliers. This is your opportunity to sample the wares of British Columbia’s finest and sometimes most obscure breweries, such as Burnaby-based Dageraad and Howe Sound of Squamish.

Almost directly opposite Drake is Fan Tan Alley. Narrow, uneven, and very photogenic, its northern end leads to Fisgard Street and Canada’s oldest Chinatown. Continue across Fisgard to the atmospheric Dragon Alley. From there, it is just a quick two blocks further on Government Street to arrive at Phillips Brewing and Malting.

Another of Victoria’s breweries that branched into distilling, 25 year old Phillips Brewing added a distillery in 2014 and its own malting plant a year later, making it one of the very few brewery-distillery-maltings in North America, and perhaps the only one in a city center. A partnership with local sandwich legend Roast has elevated the taproom menu and aesthetic, while the addition of distiller-blender Kevin Titcomb has helped improve the distillery’s Sanctuary Signature Edition single malt—a light but lively and complex blend of 5 to 9 year old whiskies aged in whisky, wine, and beer casks.

A few blocks around the Upper Harbour, in Victoria’s more industrial district, is the Brass Monkey Taproom, formerly Moon Under Water. Visitors can sample the full assortment of Brass Monkey beers and Moon spirits, but the diverse range of Antifogmatic Bliss whiskies, whether corn, rye, malted barley, or wheat, is not to be missed.

A visit to Macaloney’s Island Distillery does require a taxi or rideshare, but as one of Canada’s finest whisky producers, it’s well worth the journey. Scottish ex-pat founder Graeme Macaloney is the master distiller, and his devotion to single pot still and single malt whisky is unwavering. Of particular note is the Peat Project range, featuring malts smoked on-premise with Pacific Northwest peat.

No trip to Victoria is complete without a visit to Clive’s Classic Lounge and Strath Liquor Merchants, respectively the city’s finest whisky bar and shop, conveniently located around the corner from one another. Add a meal at the nearby, very BC whisky-friendly Courtney Room, and your journey to western Canada’s whisky paradise will be complete.

Hit the Road, Whisky Lover

Outside of Victoria proper, the 150 coastal miles between the city and Campbell River to the north offer a quartet of creative, innovative, and impressive whisky distilleries, beginning with Shelter Point at the northernmost end.

Shelter Point is a true farm-to-bottle operation, growing the majority of the barley it uses. Its flagship 7 year old Classic single malt can rival many of Scotland’s youthful coastal- influenced whiskies, but visitors would be advised to explore the distillery’s more limited releases, like the fruity marzipan-and marmalade-accented 12 year old and the alligator- char oak-aged Ripple Rock single malts.

Just a half-hour south in Courtney is Wayward Distillery, which claims to have been the first distillery in Canada to produce spirits from honey, and donates 1% of its sales to Pollinator Partnership Canada in appreciation of the bees. Its flagship is the floral, buttery Drunken Hive rum, but equally noteworthy is the distillery’s newer whisky program that includes the bourbon-style Unruly Suburban, with sweet and fruity charred oak aromas and a full body that seems more akin to Tennessee whiskey than bourbon.

An hour south of Wayward, in Nanaimo, is Arbutus Distillery & Cocktail Lounge, where single malt whisky shares the stage with a 100% Canadian rye and a blend of separately distilled and aged barley, wheat, and rye whiskies aptly called Canadian 3-Grain. For aficionados of lighter Lowland malts, its Canadian single malt will check several boxes, while the rye sits halfway between the relatively soft Canadian approach and the punchier American straight version. It’s with the 3-Grain, however, that the distillery has really hit its stride, with an attractive citrus-spice nose and medium-bodied orange toffee palate.

An overnight stop in Nanaimo makes for a fine respite from a day of driving and tasting, and provides the opportunity to sample several versions of that famous Canadian sweet, the Nanaimo bar. This is a three-layer square with a base of graham cracker, coconut, and cocoa, a middle layer of custard cream, and a top layer of chocolate ganache, and is almost as popular as the butter tart. Consider the Coast Bastion Hotel as a base, convenient to the city’s Art Gallery and Nanaimo Museum, with higher floors providing stellar views.

The final southward stop is Stillhead Distillery in Duncan, about 45 minutes from Nanaimo. Not quite a decade old, Stillhead has made a name for itself with intriguing cask finishes, like its limited spring release Garry Oak single grain rye, aged 3 1/2 years in charred oak before being finished in once-used barrels crafted from Quercus garryana, the Garry oak, which imbues the whisky with a deep color, clove aroma, and vaguely rum-like character, minus the sweetness. Not to be missed is the distillery’s flagship Islay Cask single grain rye, with a smoked herb aroma and rich flavors of salt, spice, plum, and smoke.

IF YOU GO

Flights to Victoria typically connect through Vancouver, except for Alaska Airlines, which flies direct from Seattle, and numerous Canadian airlines that fly direct from major Canadian hubs. Harbour Air offers frequent downtown-to-downtown service from Vancouver.

Ferries operate from Seattle and Port Angeles, Washington, as well as from Tsawwassen, BC, about 45 minutes from the U.S. border. If walking rather than driving onto the ferry, passengers can take a BC Transit bus or taxi into the city, or rent a car at the terminal.

Driving is unnecessary in central Victoria, as the compact downtown is easy to traverse on foot. In inclement weather or for longer distances, public transit, electric taxis, bike rentals, and rideshares are all options.

Suggested hotels include the historic Fairmont Empress, the luxurious Magnolia and Grand Pacific, more budget-friendly Strathcona—home to the Strath—and cottagey Spinnakers.

In addition to distilleries, the city is home to a large number of highly accomplished breweries, including Hoyne, Île Sauvage, Whistle Buoy, and Herald Street, and is considered a whale-watching paradise, with numerous companies offering tours. For the horticulturally inclined, the world-famous 55-acre Butchart Gardens is a must. With its impressive scenery and attractions, Victoria appeals to every visitor, whisky lovers included.
rye-whiskey-reviews-summer-2020:
Bourbon may be America's native spirit, but rye was famous first, dominating the national market until the mid-19th century. When Prohibition shut down America's thriving whiskey industry, rye's popularity sank. But over the last couple decades, rye whiskey has come roaring back thanks in large part to the cocktail renaissance.Rye is a traditional flavoring grain in both American and Canadian whiskies and often adds a punch of spice, even when used in small amounts. In the U.S., rye whiskey must have at least 51% rye in its mashbill, resulting in a spirit that's less sweet than bourbon, with bold aromas and flavors. And because rye often reaches maturity quicker than bourbon, even new distilleries can produce superb bottlings.Whisky Advocate's Summer 2020 Buying Guide offers reviews of more than 130 whiskies, including over a dozen ryes. From cask-strength offerings to innovative cask finishes—plus the first taste of the newly revamped Old Overholt—there's a whiskey for just about every type of rye fan. And for even more rye, check out the issue's guide to soaking in the charms of Pittsburgh, the epicenter of the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794, and ground zero for Monongahela rye.Pour a glass of one of these zesty whiskeys—or stir up a wicked Manhattan—as you contemplate your next rye-ward jaunt, whether it's to the birthplace of this bold spirit or your local liquor store.

Spice Up Your Summertime Sipping With These Rye Whiskeys


Barrell 4 year old Cask Strength Rye (Batch 003)—93 points, 58.35% ABV, $90There's much to discover in the depths of this glass, which continues to develop over time. Dark fruit, tobacco, orange pekoe tea, white pepper, leather, dry-roasted peanuts, and varnish unfold on the nose, while the palate is fruity with blackberry, raspberry, blueberry, and orange; it also has dry oak, nuts, tobacco, and a lot of black pepper spice. The finish is leathery and peppery, with cigar and persistent dark berry flavors. A dense, decadent whiskey that makes it all seem effortless. (12,000 bottles) —Susannah Skiver Barton
Hudson Manhattan Straight Rye (Batch 5)—91 points, 46% ABV, $50A well-choreographed interplay of rich dark fruit—plums, Luxardo cherries, Concord grapes—and deep spices on the nose, along with hints of wood char and licorice; it turns tropical and nutty when water is added. The palate is richly spiced—cedar, ginger, cloves, allspice—and silky with extra-dark chocolate, grilled plums, espresso beans, and hints of aged cigar. It ends rich and toasty, with lush oak, hookah tobacco, and coffee bean. —Susannah Skiver Barton
Sagamore Spirit Calvados Cask-Finished Rye—91 points, 50.6% ABV, $69Mature but lively character; it has dark fruit, black tea, mint oil, fennel seed, and licorice on the nose. The palate is brawny and robust—it practically eats water—and swells with mint, licorice, root beer, black pepper, baking spice, espresso, and grape Robitussin. The lengthy finish is peppery and rich, with oak, herbs, baking spice, tea leaves, and dark chocolate. —Susannah Skiver Barton
Wood's 2 year old Alpine Rye (Batch 16)—91 points, 49% ABV, $55From Colorado-based Wood's High Mountain Distillery. A nose of apple, brown sugar, and blackcurrant, set against jalapeño spice and smoke. The palate offers flavors of cinnamon and burnt espresso beans, with an alluring smoky bitterness and notes of jalapeño, smoked chiles, and black pepper. On the finish, dried dark fruits and bitter chocolate emerge, with a blast of pepper at the end. Rich, brawny, and assertive, but also supple and well integrated. —David Fleming
Belfour Spirits Limited Edition Straight Rye—89 points, 50% ABV, $299A nose of lemon drops, tea leaves, light barrel char, and herb-garden notes. The palate is honeyed, with lemon, licorice, herbs, and earthiness, balancing against vanilla cream and spice, all integrating well with the barrel. A lengthy finish is well-textured and spiced, highlighted by notes of tobacco, herbs, and chocolate. Creamy, spicy, and a bit unusual, this whiskey offers spiced complexity and impressive flavor balance on the palate. —David Fleming
Old Overholt Straight Rye—87 points, 43% ABV, $18Sweet cherries, bubble gum, and fresh blueberry on the nose, along with nougat, honey-roasted peanuts, and milk chocolate. The palate has flavors of clove-studded orange, spice, and the chewed end of a pencil. It's light-bodied and verges on thin when water is added, so be judicious. The finish is gentle, with peppery oak, cinnamon, and espresso bean. This is a new higher proof and the whiskey is now non-chill filtered, so don't be surprised by a little haze if you add water or ice. —Susannah Skiver BartonBonus Scores: Check out nine more rye whiskeys from Summer, including Elijah Craig Kentucky Straight Rye, an Editors' Choice.
5-speyside-adventures:
Home to more than 45 single malt distilleries, Speyside is a whisky lover's paradise. You could visit the area for weeks and never run out of whisky-related activities. But Speyside offers more than just delicious drams, so be sure to make time for an adventure or two.

Walk this Way

The Speyside Way, a 65-mile route following the Spey Valley, links the Moray Coast with the Grampian Mountains. The breathtaking hike is dotted with distilleries and great whisky bars.

Engineer a Tour

Hop aboard and take a nostalgic eleven-mile railroad ride from the distillery town of Keith to Dufftown,the whisky capital of Speyside.

Ride in Style

A chauffeur-driven Range Rover Vogue will ferry you around the whisky sites of Speyside with in-depth tours tailored to fulfill all your Speyside whisky desires.

Float your Boat

Hop into a canoe for a leisurely 50 to 70-mile descent of the River Spey to the Moray coast. Personalized whisky tastings and distillery tours along the way make it quite an oar-deal.

Hit the Trail

The Speyside Malt Whisky Trail includes seven working distilleries, the working Speyside Cooperage, and Dallas Dhu, a closed historic distillery preserved as a museum.
new-whiskeys-from-bookers-jack-daniels-a:
It's an American whiskey-heavy week for new releases, kicking off with the latest batch of Booker's. Joining it is a wheater from New Riff, two new bourbons from Iron Smoke, and a high-rye bourbon from Liberty Pole. Elsewhere, Jack Daniel's has debuted another Single Barrel Special Release rye, Pursuit United has a new double oak rye, Chattanooga Whiskey has its first-ever Tennessee whiskeys, and Penelope has the fifth iteration of its collaborative blend with FCancer. Overseas, Bowmore has partnered with a New York-based design firm on two new single malts. 

Booker’s 2026 Batch No. 3 The Southern Thunder Batch Bourbon

ABV: 63.65%
SRP: $100
Availability: Limited

The third Booker’s batch of the year has arrived. It comprises five different production dates, with the youngest at 7 years old, stored throughout five seven-story warehouses. The barrel breakdown is as follows:

  • 23% matured on the 5th floor of warehouse 3
  • 21% matured on the 3rd floor of warehouse G
  • 22% matured on the 6th floor of warehouse 6
  • 20% matured on the 4th floor of warehouse 4
  • 14% matured on the 4th floor of warehouse M

As with every new batch of Booker’s, this one comes with a story about its namesake, late master distiller Booker Noe. Many who knew Booker described him as “Southern thunder,” because of his deep, booming voice.

Jack Daniel’s Single Barrel Special Release Coy Hill Rye (2026 Release)

ABV: 64.35%–74.25%
SRP: $90
Availability: Nationwide

Jack Daniel’s latest Single Barrel Special Release has arrived. This year’s edition is another rye, following in the footsteps of last year’s debut of Tanyard Hill. These barrels were distilled in 2016 and aged for 10 years on Coy Hill—the highest point of elevation at the distillery—in Barrelhouses 1–13. It uses Jack’s signature rye mashbill of 70% rye, 18% corn, and 12% malted barley, and it underwent the Lincoln County process.

Chattanooga Whiskey Bad Chattanoogan Tennessee Whiskey

ABV: 50%
SRP: $65
Availability: Limited

For its first Tennessee whiskey, Chattanooga Whiskey stayed true to its experimental roots, finishing it with toasted maple wood records (yes, you read that right). The straight Tennessee whiskey is made from three high-malt mashbills, maple charcoal mellowed, and aged 4 years in oak. After this initial maturation, the whiskey was transferred to barrels along with records cut from solid sugar maple; they were toasted for a day and laser-engraved with two original tribute songs about the distillery written by Chattanooga Whiskey creative director Rich Abercrombie, who also fronts the Dollars Family band. The whiskey was finished for 30 days.

Bad Chattanoogan comes in two editions: Side A, “Bad Chattanoogan,” and Side B, “City I Love.” Each bottle comes with a playable four-inch Tiny Vinyl hangtag featuring both original songs. The whiskeys are available at seelbachs.com and at Tennessee retailers.

Given that Chattanooga is a Tennessee-based distillery, it may come as a surprise that this is its first Tennessee whiskey; until now, it had forgone the Lincoln County Process, the hallmark of Tennessee whiskey.

ABV: 50%
SRP: $60
Availability: Limited

Newport, Kentucky-based New Riff has unveiled a new wheated bourbon. The mashbill—65% corn, 18% floor-malted wheat, 10% unmalted wheat, and 7% dark wheat—is likened to a beer recipe, drawing on the distilling team's brewing background. The use of floor-malted wheat, a labor-intensive process, is intended to lend the bourbon greater depth and a more robust character. Bottled in bond without chill filtration, the release is available exclusively to New Riff's Whiskey Club members, with pickup at the distillery.

ABV: 50.5%
SRP: $80
Availability: Nationwide

Now in its fifth year of collaboration with FCancer, Penelope Bourbon has released its annual limited-edition whiskey, this year a 6 year old blend of straight bourbon and American malt whiskeys. Distilled at parent company MGP's distillery in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, the whiskey features a four-grain mashbill of 64% corn, 20% rye, 1% malted rye, and 15% malted barley. Previous releases have featured blends of straight whiskeys, while last year's Batch 4 also included a cask-strength iteration. The brand has pledged $250,000 to the nonprofit that advocates for cancer prevention and early detection.

The inaugural release is a barrel proof rye, blending straight rye whiskeys from Bardstown Bourbon Company and Sagamore Spirit before undergoing almost 2 years of additional maturation in American oak barrels from Seguin Moreau's Napa cooperage. The barrels feature a no.-3 char and toasted heads, a combination previously used in its single barrel release, Episode 063. This release is just 720 bottles, with 92% allocated to existing Pursuit’s club (P. Club) members and the remainder reserved for new members who join in person at the brand's Whiskey Row location in Louisville.

Collecting-Japanese-Whisky:
There are plenty of reasons to collect Japanese whiskies, not least the steady flow of high-end collectibles that enter the retail market. Keep an eye on the 2024 Tsukuriwake Series from the House of Suntory, which includes four limited-edition bottlings from Yamazaki and Hakushu. The previous Tsukuriwake release in 2022 attracted significant auction interest, whether sold as a set or individually. Between 2021-23, Nikka Whisky released its Discovery Series—five one-off exploratory bottlings that showed the impact of different yeasts on aromas created during fermentation, the making of peated whisky at a distillery known for its unpeated style, and the blending of aged grain whiskies, among other experiments. Nikka Nine Decades, a world blend of whiskies from every decade stretching back to the 1940s from six Nikka-owned distilleries, was released for the company’s 90th anniversary and will undoubtedly attract collectors.

The Japanese whisky auction record was previously held by Karuizawa 1960 52 year old and editions of Yamazaki 50 year old, but the current record holder is Yamazaki 55 year old. It attracted a hammer price of $645,125 at Bonhams, Hong Kong in 2020 and can still fetch over $200,000 at auction, but several bottles have not sold this year after failing to reach their reserve. Japanese whisky at auction took off internationally as a collectible over the past 5–10 years, spurred on to new heights by bottlings of the last casks from Karuizawa and Hanyu. Many bottles remain in circulation and turn up at auction regularly, but be cautious around any bottlings with easily replaced wax seals, as many lack dependable security features. Auctioneers often spot color variations between bottlings purportedly from the same batch, which has led to questions about provenance and authenticity.

Blended Japanese whisky, especially Hibiki limited editions, commands some of the highest auction prices for any blends, including scotch. Japanese single malt is the other best bet, but koji whisky has yet to make much of an impact beyond some savvy bidders seizing a good deal. It’s worth remembering that koji whisky is only sold as whisky in the U.S., but that national exclusivity is a double-edged sword. Drinkers of Japanese whisky may be curious to try them, but as these cannot legally be called whisky in other countries, it’s likely their value will be far lower as a result.

Finally, Japan’s distillery construction boom brings plenty of scope for building up a modern collection. Chichibu is a sought-after collectible with a vast array of single cask editions and limited labels, but it’s popular, and there are few bargains. Early releases from young distilleries showing real promise are worthy of your consideration too, such as Shizuoka, Akkeshi, and Kanosuke. If nothing else, the payback for early adopters will be knowing that each fledgling distillery release they acquire captures a valuable moment of liquid history.

Japanese whisky at auction took off internationally as a collectible over the past 5-10 years, spurred on to new heights by bottlings of the last casks from Karuizawa and Hanyu.
